stem: A 52-year-old man with a 30 pack-year smoking history, who quit 10 years ago, comes for a routine checkup. He has no symptoms. What is the most appropriate screening test?
expl: USPSTF: annual low-dose CT for adults 50–80 years with ≥20 pack-years who currently smoke or quit within the past 15 years. He is 52, 30 pack-years, quit 10 years ago → eligible.

why.B: Sputum cytology isn't a screening test.
why.D: PET is for staging, not screening.

stem: A patient with colorectal cancer is being evaluated for tumor recurrence. What is the most appropriate tumor marker to assess recurrence?
expl: CEA is the colorectal cancer marker used to detect recurrence after resection (a rise suggests recurrence).

stem: What is the reason for sentinel lymph node biopsy in surgical breast cancer?

opts.t: To guide the radiation therapy decision
Assess the extent of lymphatic involvement
To assess tumor staging and prognosis

expl: Sentinel lymph node biopsy samples the first draining node(s) to find out whether the axilla is involved — i.e. the extent of lymphatic spread — without a full axillary dissection.

why.A: Radiation decisions may follow, but that's not its purpose.
why.C: Staging is a consequence; the direct purpose is assessing nodal involvement.
why.D: Same — chemo decisions follow from the result.

stem: Which of the following can be the candidate for lung cancer screening

opts.t: a 51 year-old male with 30 pack-year smoking
a 52 year-old male with 10 pack-year smoking
a 40 year-old male with 20 pack-year smoking
a 49 year-old male with 20 pack-year smoking

expl: Eligibility = age 50–80 AND ≥20 pack-years (current smoker or quit ≤15 years). Only the 51-year-old with 30 pack-years meets both. (The source writes "correct answer is A".)

stem: patient presents for screening colonoscopy. The patient has no family history of colon cancer. What is the most appropriate recommendation for age to do colonoscopy ?

opts.t: Screening colonoscopy every 10 years at age 45- 50

expl: Average-risk adults start colorectal screening at 45 (older guidelines 50); colonoscopy is repeated every 10 years if normal. Age 40 is for those with a first-degree relative (or 10 years before the relative's diagnosis).

why.B: That start age is for increased-risk (family history) patients.

stem: There was a patient with incurable cancer. The case was discussed in the tumor board, and the family asked about the palliative surgery, why would you do surgery for incurable cancer?

opts.t: Improved quality of life is an indication of surgery

expl: Palliative surgery aims to relieve symptoms (obstruction, bleeding, pain) and improve quality of life, not to cure.

why.B: Wishes matter, but the indication is symptom relief/QoL.
why.C: Survival benefit is not the goal of palliation.

stem: 89 year old patient presents with 3 day history of inability to pass flatus, she previously had 5 months constipation imaging revealed obstruction in sigmoid colon with no distended small bowel. She has multiple liver and lung metastases. What is the management
expl: Source key: colectomy — a palliative resection of the obstructing sigmoid tumor relieves the obstruction and prevents bleeding/perforation; many would also accept a stent or colostomy in an 89-year-old with metastases. Follow the source key for the exam.

why.C: A defunctioning colostomy is a reasonable alternative.
why.D: A stent is another palliative option, especially in frail patients.

stem: A patient had cancer and she was cured of it, the patient asked the doctor how we can make sure the cancer is cured and when.

opts.t: Normal duration of life without further clinical or radiological evidence
No microscopic deposits of tumor is present

expl: Cure is judged clinically: the patient lives a normal life span without clinical or radiological evidence of recurrence. You cannot prove "no microscopic cells".

stem: Rule of adjuvant chemotherapy

opts.t: Has no role in improving mortality

expl: Adjuvant chemotherapy is systemic — it treats micrometastases (systemic control) and also lowers local recurrence.

why.B: Chemo is systemic, not only local.
why.C: It also contributes to local control.

stem: Which of the following is true regarding cancer screening.

opts.t: Detect cancer in its early stages when treatment is possible

expl: Screening aims to detect cancer early, when treatment is still effective; a screening test needs high sensitivity.

stem: 54 years old male diagnosed and treated for Prostate cancer which of the following biomarkers would be helpful during follow up ?
expl: PSA is used in screening, diagnosis and especially follow-up after prostate-cancer treatment (a rising PSA = biochemical recurrence).

stem: A 30-year-old female diagnosed as hepatocellular carcinoma 4 cm in size with child's B cirrhosis. Which of the following is the best treatment option?

opts.t: Hepatic resection with 2 cm margin of normal live

srcNote: (Transplant surgery) Source note (436 A Q31): Milan criteria: Cirrhosis + child B + single nodule size <5cm = transplant Milan criteria (a set of criteria used to assess HCC patients for transplant) 1 tumor measuring � 2 cm and � 5 cm OR 2-3 tumors measuring � 1 cm and � 3 cm
expl: Milan criteria: single tumor ≤5 cm or up to 3 tumors ≤3 cm, no vascular invasion. Child B cirrhosis + 4 cm HCC → transplant.

why.A: Resection is unsafe in Child B cirrhosis.
why.C: RFA is for small tumors (<3 cm) and doesn't treat cirrhosis.

stem: A 65 years old patient with HCC 3 cm and positive HCV. Which of the following is the best treatment option?

opts.t: Hepatic resection with 2 cm margin of normal liver

expl: HCC 3 cm on an HCV-cirrhotic liver within Milan criteria → transplant treats both the tumor and the cirrhosis.

why.B: RFA is an option for small HCC/bridging, but transplant is best when eligible.
why.C: Resection in a cirrhotic liver risks liver failure and leaves the diseased liver.

stem: BRCA1 is seen commonly with which cancer?
expl: BRCA1 mutations predispose mainly to breast (and ovarian) cancer.

stem: In the management of colorectal cancer, what is CEA most useful for?

opts.t: To assess the prognosis of colorectal cancer
To assess severity of cancer aggressiveness
For surveillance of recurrent colorectal cancer

expl: CEA is not sensitive/specific enough for screening; its main use is follow-up for recurrence.

why.B: A high pre-op CEA has prognostic value, but the main use is surveillance.

stem: What is the diagnostic tumor marker used in pre-treatment in thyroid cancer?
expl: Source key: calcitonin — the pre-treatment diagnostic marker for medullary thyroid cancer. Thyroglobulin isn't diagnostic before surgery (benign thyroid tissue makes it); it is used for follow-up after total thyroidectomy in papillary/follicular cancer.

stem: A 55 years old male with locally advanced low rectal cancer (T3N1M0) with no obstructive symptoms. Which of the following options is the best treatment option to start with?
expl: Locally advanced low rectal cancer (T3N1) → neoadjuvant (chemo)radiation first to down-stage and reduce local recurrence, then surgery.

why.C: Upfront surgery has higher local recurrence in T3N1 low rectal cancer.
why.D: Chemo alone is part of TNT but radiation is the keyed start.

stem: A 65-year-old male presented to the emergency room with a picture of bowel obstruction. A CT scan of the abdomen showed an ultra low rectal mass with bi-lobar liver metastasis, lung metastasis as well as retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy. Which or the following is the best management option for his current condition?
expl: Obstruction from an ultra-low rectal mass with widespread metastases → palliate the obstruction with a diverting stoma. Ultra-low tumors are not suitable for stents (tenesmus, pain, migration).

why.C: Stents are poor for ultra-low rectal tumors.

stem: A 70 year old lady presents to the hospital with a history of passing bright red blood mixed with stool for 3 weeks. Review of systems reveals low appetite, constipation and approximately 4kg weight loss in 2 months. She denies abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting and fever, but she feels lethargic. On examination, she is pale. Vital signs: BP: 110/70, pulse 92/min and temperature: 37, and oxygen saturation is 92% on room air. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Elderly patient, rectal bleeding mixed with stool, change in bowel habit, weight loss and anemia → colorectal cancer until proven otherwise.

why.C: Diverticulitis presents with LLQ pain and fever.
why.D: IBD usually presents younger with diarrhea.

stem: What is the tumor marker for colorectal cancer?
expl: CEA = colorectal.

stem: What is the tumor marker for pancreatic head tumor?
expl: CA 19-9 is the pancreatic (and biliary) tumor marker ("CA19-1" here is a typo for 19-9).

stem: A 40-year old patient presented to the ER after vomiting blood, endoscopy showed a mass in the stomach which was submucosal with normal covering and ulcerating in the middle stomach, which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: A submucosal mass covered by normal mucosa with central ulceration ("umbilication") that bleeds is classic for GIST.

why.C: Adenocarcinoma arises from the mucosa, so the mucosa is abnormal.
why.D: Linitis plastica = diffuse infiltrating "leather bottle" stomach.

stem: Rectal cancer stage T3c N1 with no mets, given chemoradiation as neoadjuvant. the radiation role is:
expl: Neoadjuvant chemoradiation in T3 rectal cancer down-stages the tumor (making resection easier/sphincter-saving) and reduces local recurrence. Source key: down-stage.

why.B: Also a true benefit; the keyed answer is down-staging.
why.C: Radiation is local; it doesn't reduce distant recurrence.
why.D: Overall survival benefit is not proven.

stem: Which of the following is a tumor marker for prostate cancer?
expl: PSA = prostate.

stem: BRCA1 found in which cancer?
expl: BRCA1 = breast (and ovarian) cancer.

why.D: BRCA2 more than BRCA1 is linked to prostate; breast is the classic answer.

stem: Carcino-embryonic antigen (CEA) in the blood, Can be used and helpful in colorectal cancer for what ?
expl: CEA is used to watch for recurrence after colorectal cancer treatment.

why.B: Has some prognostic value but not the main use.

stem: 58 Year Old Male came to hospital with obstructive symptoms, CT showed Rectosigmoid obstruction and secondary liver and lung deposit. What would you do?

opts.t: Nothing as there is secondary deposit

expl: Obstructing rectosigmoid cancer with liver and lung metastases → palliate the obstruction with a defunctioning (transverse) colostomy.

why.C: Bypass is less practical for a rectosigmoid tumor.
why.D: The obstruction must be relieved regardless of metastases.

stem: Neoadjuvant Radiotherapy role in colon cancer is?
expl: Radiotherapy is a local treatment → its role is local control (reducing local recurrence).

why.C: Systemic control is the role of chemotherapy.

stem: A 62 year old man presented to the outpatient department complaining of hematochezia for 3 months. Physical examination revealed third degree hemorrhoids. Which of the following is an appropriate initial step in management?
expl: Hematochezia in a 62-year-old must be investigated with colonoscopy to exclude colorectal cancer, even if hemorrhoids are found.

why.A: Treating before excluding cancer is wrong.

stem: You just complete an oncologic resection procedure on a patient and plan to start that patient on chemotherapy. How long should you ideally wait before starting the first cycle of chemotherapy to minimize the chances of wound healing problems?
srcNote: (Skin and soft tissue lesions) (From a wound healing perspective the third phase of wound healing is completed by the third week and it is the phase most susceptible to factors that delay wound healing such as chemotherapy, thus starting chemotherapy after 3 weeks ensures wound healing does not get delayed, therefore the answer is B)(Essentials of plastic book had a question with the same scenario and the answer was to wait for 10-14 days to minimize healing problems)
expl: Chemotherapy impairs the proliferative phase of wound healing; starting ~3 weeks after surgery avoids wound problems (other sources say 10–14 days).

stem: A 52-year-old woman who is known to have Hashimoto's thyroiditis for 12 years, presented to the outpatient department complaining of progressive anterior neck swelling with stridor for 3 months. Examination revealed diffuse, large non- tender thyroid swelling with retrosternal extension. She underwent a core needle biopsy. Ultrasound: diffuse thyroid enlargement, causing bilateral carotid sheath. Histopathology: Malignant thyroid tumor. Which of the following is the most likely tumor?
srcNote: (Thyroid gland) The most likely malignancy associated with Hashimoto’s thyroiditis is lymphoma
expl: Long-standing Hashimoto's thyroiditis is the main risk factor for primary thyroid lymphoma, which presents as a rapidly enlarging goitre with compressive symptoms.

why.B: Anaplastic is rapid too, but the Hashimoto's link points to lymphoma.

stem: Woman with colon cancer underwent resection and had chemo after surgery. What is the type of chemo?
expl: Chemotherapy given after surgery = adjuvant.

stem: What is the most likely diagnosis of the picture:
srcNote: (Skin and soft tissue lesions) Source figure: 435 A Q25 Source figure: 435 A Q25
expl: Source key: SCC (ulcerated lesion with everted margins in the picture).

why.A: BCC has a rolled pearly edge and rarely ulcerates widely.

stem: What sample is taken for parathyroid cancer?
expl: Parathyroid carcinoma is diagnosed at surgery (frozen section/en bloc resection). FNA is avoided because of the risk of seeding the tract.

why.D: FNA risks seeding and can't distinguish adenoma from carcinoma.

stem: A 62 y.o male presented to OPD C/O early satiety and wt. loss (11kg) for the last 3 months. Physical examination was unremarkable. Upper GI endoscopy with multiple biopsies has been taken: Histopathology:gastric adenocarcinoma, Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
expl: After biopsy-proven gastric adenocarcinoma, the first staging step is CT chest/abdomen/pelvis to look for metastases; if no distant disease → EUS (T/N stage) and diagnostic laparoscopy (peritoneal spread) for locally advanced tumours.

why.A: Done after CT for local staging.
why.C: After CT, for T3/T4 or node-positive disease.

stem: Which of the following infecting organism carries the risk of upper GI contamination and neoplastic diseases?
srcNote: (Acute abdomen) Source note (429 F Q52): Helicobacter pylori is the commonest cause of peptic ulceration and gastric adenocarcinoma world wide. Reference: Davidson 6th ed. ch. 13 p. 171
expl: H. pylori colonizes the upper GI tract and causes peptic ulcer, gastric adenocarcinoma and MALT lymphoma.

stem: A 73 y/o lady presented to the emergency department with bright red blood mixed with the stool for 3 weeks. Review of systems reveals low appetite, constipation and approximately 4kg weigh loss on 2 months. She denies abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting and fever, but she feels lethargic. Temperature: 37 0C, and oxygen saturation is 92% on room air. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Same picture as the classic colon cancer scenario → adenocarcinoma.

why.C: UC presents with bloody diarrhea, younger.
why.D: Diverticulosis bleeds painlessly but doesn't cause weight loss.

stem: Regarding breast cancer which ONE of the following is the single most important prognostic factor?

opts.t: Number of involved axillary lymph nodes

srcNote: (breast cancer) Traumatic Head Injury and Intracranial Bleeding
expl: The single most important prognostic factor in breast cancer is the axillary lymph-node status (number of involved nodes).

stem: A 67-year-old male presented with per-rectal bleeding since 6 months with unremarkable physical examination. Colonoscopy revealed ulcerating mass in the splenic flexure, confirmed by histopathology to be adenocarcinoma. Which of the following is recommended for staging of this cancer?

opts.t: CT scan chest, abdomen and pelvis

srcNote: (liver and splenic diseases and pancreatic masses)
expl: Colon cancer staging = CT chest, abdomen and pelvis (+ CEA). MRI pelvis is for rectal cancer.

stem: Premalignant polyp
expl: Adenomatous polyps follow the adenoma–carcinoma sequence.

why.A: Most hamartomatous polyps are not premalignant (except in syndromes).
why.C: Hyperplastic polyps are generally not premalignant.

stem: Staging of the colon cancer:
expl: Colon cancer staging = CT chest/abdomen/pelvis (liver, lung, peritoneum).

why.C: MRI is for rectal local staging/liver lesions.

stem: Definitive increase risk for colon cancer:
expl: Long-standing UC carries a clearly increased colorectal cancer risk (Crohn's colitis does too, but UC is the classic answer).

why.A: Not equal in the classic teaching.

stem: One of these is a malignant tumor of the lung:
expl: Carcinoid is a malignant (low-grade) neuroendocrine lung tumor. Cysts and hamartomas are benign.

stem: all are a predisposition for esophageal cancer except:
expl: Achalasia, Plummer-Vinson, Barrett's and corrosive injury all predispose to esophageal cancer; a simple esophageal cyst does not.

stem: patient with suspected brain tumor the initial investigation to be done:
expl: Old key: CT is the initial (quick, available) investigation; MRI is the best study to characterize a brain tumor.

why.B: Myelography is for the spinal canal.

stem: In breast cancer prognosis depend mainly on:

opts.t: number of positive axillary lymph node

expl: The number of positive axillary nodes is the most important prognostic factor in breast cancer.

why.B: Important but less than nodal status.
why.C: Important but less than nodal status.

stem: patient came to the hospital with a mass over her neck, examination and ultrasound revealed a nodule within the thyroid. What is the most appropriate next step:
expl: Thyroid nodule → FNA (after TSH) to decide benign vs malignant.

why.D: TSH is checked, but FNA is the diagnostic step keyed.

stem: malignant tumor that arise from the parafollicular C cells:
expl: Parafollicular C cells make calcitonin → medullary carcinoma.

stem: commonest malignant melanoma:
expl: Superficial spreading melanoma is the commonest type (~70%).

stem: palpable gallbladder: Tumor of the head of the pancreas Stone in CBD
expl: In CBD stones the gallbladder is usually fibrosed/shrunken from chronic cholecystitis, so it isn't palpable.
ansText: Tumor of the head of the pancreas (Courvoisier's law: a palpable gallbladder with painless jaundice is unlikely to be due to stones).

stem: Paget disease:
srcNote: not complete Q, they think it’s A (Surgical oncology)
expl: Paget's disease of the nipple is an eczema-like change of the nipple that reflects an underlying breast carcinoma (in situ or invasive).

stem: Fibroadenoma:
expl: The question is incomplete in the source; the facts above are what was being tested.
ansText: Both listed statements are false: fibroadenomas are usually <3–5 cm (giant >5 cm is uncommon) and they are well encapsulated, mobile ("breast mouse").

stem: Cholangiocarcinoma “incomplete Q”

opts.t: is most commonly in Bifurcation of hepatic duct

expl: Cholangiocarcinoma most commonly arises at the hepatic duct bifurcation (hilar/Klatskin tumor, ~60%).

stem: All liver cyst except “not complete Q”
expl: The question is incomplete; the keyed fact is that metastases are the commonest malignant liver lesions (and are not true cysts).

why.B: Colon cancer is a common source of liver metastases.

stem: Paraneoplastic syndrome for hepatocellular carcinoma cause all except
srcNote: , paraneoplastic syndromes (PNS) which have been associated with HCC include hypercholesterolemia, hypercalcemia, erythrocytosis, hypoglycemia, demyelinating disease, pemphigus, polyarthritis, encephalomyelitis, and thrombocytosis
expl: HCC paraneoplastic syndromes include hypoglycemia, hypercalcemia, hypercholesterolemia and erythrocytosis — not hyperglycemia. ("Hypocholesterolemia" in option D is also not typical; the keyed answer is A.)

stem: All can predispose to hepatocellular cancer except
srcNote: , it’s the least risk Source figure: 426 F Q17
expl: Cirrhosis and hepatitis B/C cause HCC. Hepatitis A does not cause chronic liver disease — yet the source keyed smoking as "the least risk". Know both facts.

why.C: Hepatitis A doesn't cause chronic infection or HCC.

stem: old lady. she has firm fixed swelling in her right neck, in the posterior triangle, behind the middle part of SCM muscle. what's the best initial investigation?
expl: Source key: thyroid nuclear scan, but the compilers thought cervical CT is right. A firm, fixed posterior-triangle mass in an elderly patient is most likely a metastatic node — the work-up is imaging (CT neck) plus FNA and a search for the primary (often head & neck).

why.A: Laryngoscopy is part of searching for a primary, not the first test.

stem: Parotid malignant feature
expl: Features of a malignant parotid tumor: skin ulceration/fixation, facial nerve palsy, rapid growth, cervical nodes.

why.C: Pain suggests inflammation (though it can occur in malignancy).

stem: Marjolijn ulcer “incomplete question” probably they meant what type of cancer it’s most likely associated with
expl: Long-standing scars/ulcers undergo malignant change to SCC.
ansText: SCC — a Marjolin ulcer is an aggressive squamous cell carcinoma arising in a chronic wound or burn scar.

stem: Esophageal not precancerous “I think they’re asking which of the following condition is not precancerous”
expl: Plummer-Vinson, achalasia and Barrett's are premalignant; a cyst is not.

stem: Palliative treatment for esophageal cancer all except

opts.t: surgery Stent is long term effective palliative
radiotherapy high beam is very effective
Cisplatin can be used surgical palliative resection
can be used for selective patients

expl: The question is incomplete; the source key is B. Palliation of esophageal cancer uses stents, brachytherapy/radiotherapy and chemotherapy.

why.A: Option text garbled in the source.
why.C: Option text garbled in the source.
why.D: Option text garbled in the source.

stem: Esophageal cancer “I think they’re asking which is true about esophageal cancer”

opts.t: Chemo only is curative for early stage cancer
Most common symptom is progressive dysphagia
Middle and upper esophageal tumor u need to do rigid bronchoscope

expl: Progressive dysphagia (solids → liquids) is the most common presenting symptom.

why.A: Chemo alone isn't curative for early cancer.
why.C: Bronchoscopy is done for upper/middle tumors (to exclude airway invasion), but it's flexible, and B is the keyed fact.
why.D: Endoscopy is important, but B is keyed.

stem: Barret’s esophagus except
expl: Barrett's is premalignant but is managed with surveillance ± endoscopic therapy; it is not resected at the metaplasia stage.

stem: all are esophageal benign tumor except
expl: Leiomyoma (most common), fibrovascular polyp and papilloma are benign; leiomyosarcoma is malignant.
